To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the timing functions associated with age-sensitive fronto- striatal networks may be subserved by degenerate structures, such as the parietal cortex, through the use of Bayesian optimization principles.

aging is associated with increased noise, temporal uncertainty and reduced temporal precision, and that the brain’s ability to adjust to temporal uncertainty and to optimize timing performance in the presence of noise is compromised by aging.

aging is associated with a reduction in the ability to accurately and precisely estimate time intervals and that these impairments are likely to be caused by impairments in attentional and memory processes, as well as by the reduced efficiency of the central timing mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how the aging brain adapts to the increased temporal uncertainty that accompanies age-related changes in attention, memory and the possible decline in the accuracy and/or precision of the internal timing mechanism.
how aging affects timing and the mechanisms by which it does so.
understanding age-related distortions of timing and time perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the aging process is characterized by a decline in the efficiency of timing mechanisms and the emergence of a more error-prone and uncertain timing system, which is reflected in age-related distortions of time perception.
aging is associated with a decline in temporal precision, but not in the ability to perceive the passage of time, which can be explained through the use of Bayesian models and degenerate networks.
aging does not affect time perception per se, but rather the ability to perceive and estimate durations accurately and precisely.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging is associated with a loss of precision in the timing system, which may result from the reduced efficiency of the fronto-striato-cortical circuit.

the age-associated changes in timing can be explained by the combination of a more flexible Bayesian optimization model and degenerate timing mechanisms, which can be used to predict the age-associated changes and the potential interventions. aging is associated with increased uncertainty, which is associated with increased noise, which in turn is associated with increased variability in timing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aging of time perception may be a consequence of a loss of flexibility in the brain’s capacity to adapt to the statistical regularities of the environment.
the aging process is characterized by increased temporal uncertainty, which is likely to be a result of the combined effects of impairments of attention, memory and timing mechanisms.
the age-related decline in time perception is not a unitary process, but rather a complex interplay between the aging fronto-striatum and other degenerate networks.
